02INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
Editor'sColumn

Signal from the Floor

One page does not make a market report

This issue features one page outlining the South African automotive floor — not twenty. I made that correction deliberately. INSIDE MIC concerns itself with the craft of metal forming, and automotive is one customer sector among the many a stamping shop serves. A magazine that speaks only of a single industry ceases to be useful to everyone outside it, and I have sat in enough toolrooms serving appliance, mining, agricultural and packaging work to know how quickly they stop reading.

A press shop's world is larger than whichever industry happens to be loudest this week.

What earns a full page here is straightforward: material that is sourced, dated, and specific enough for a tooling shop to act upon. On the automotive side, this issue clears that bar once — a stamping facility changing ownership, and what such a change does to every tooling contract in the building. I have watched that happen from inside a supplier. The principle travels; the plant's name does not.

The remainder is the shop floor proper. What a die setter watches for that no checklist fully captures; two instalments of Die Science; and — new this issue — a three-part series on remote work through a manufacturing lens, built on the actual trials rather than the opinion pieces, because I wanted to know what the evidence said before I formed a view. A two-page feature on decentralised command closes the editorial run, and I will declare an interest: it describes a way of running a business I have practised, been misread for, and come to trust.

A word on the drawings. Every editorial page carries a figure drawn for it, because a principle in metal forming is rarely understood from prose alone. A cutting edge that meets the sheet a fraction out of square, a slug that would rather ride the punch than fall, a blank whose area must survive three draws unchanged — these are geometric facts, and geometry wants a picture. Where a photograph shows the surface, a section shows the cause. I intend to keep both.

Twenty pages is the target, built up issue by issue rather than padded out in a single sitting. Fourteen editorial pages this time, three advertisements, and the furniture that holds them together. What I would welcome most from readers is the material no research panel can supply: the fault you traced to its root last month, and the fix that held.

03INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
News &Notes

Steel quotas tighten in the EU

The EU cut tariff-free steel import quotas by ~47% effective 1 Jul 2026, doubling the out-of-quota duty to 50%. Automotive-grade coil is reported to exhaust its quota within days of opening — a direct cost line for any shop buying EU steel, not just automotive suppliers.

The hot-forming capability gap

Market analysis names hot-forming with in-die quenching — not demand — as the real barrier stopping traditional ICE-focused stamping shops from winning EV battery-tray work. The tooling knowledge is the bottleneck, not the order book.

A single-source chokepoint, made visible

A Dutch chipmaker dispute briefly cut off a components supply China controls ~75% of one input for; three major OEMs warned of production cuts within days. Worth a second look at anything in your own supply chain with exactly one source.

Gigacasting's modular swing

Large-format die casting has been displacing multi-part stamped assemblies for several years. 2026's shift toward "modular megacasting" — large cast nodes plus stamped/extruded reinforcement — reopens scope for stamped parts that a pure-casting strategy had closed off.

For the buyer's desk — four questions before the next coil order
  • Where was the coil melted and rolled — and does that origin fall inside the quota at all?
  • When does the next quota window open, and how many days did the last one last?
  • Is the out-of-quota duty priced into the RFQ, or absorbed in the margin by default?
  • Which single-source items in the bill of materials have no second supplier qualified?

CraftFeature

What a DieSetter ActuallyWatches For

The checklist gets you through an audit. It doesn't tell you what "off" sounds like.

By the Editor

A die setter's job description reads like that of any equipment role — set up, adjust, inspect, report faults. What it fails to capture is the part that actually prevents scrap. On every floor I have worked, the setter was the first person to know a die was running wrong, and usually knew it days before any checklist item would have flagged it.

The same principle underpins every sound press-maintenance programme I have seen hold up over years rather than months. The operator is the frontline defence against breakdown — not because they run the deepest diagnostics, but because they are present for every cycle, and a die or press beginning to fail announces itself first in ways a form cannot ask about: a stroke that has gone faintly sluggish, a smell that was not there yesterday, a die that "breathes" between bolster and ram at the bottom of the stroke.

  • Dies pre-staged and set precisely to the Set-Up Sheet — "close enough" is not a setting
  • Tie rods checked on a schedule — a loose rod torques the frame long before it ever produces a bad part
  • Air pressure held at the exact factory-recommended value — higher does not mean more tonnage; it means accelerated wear on seals that were never rated for it
  • Alignment discipline — the trade standard is unforgiving: roughly .001″ per linear foot, tighter again on high-speed work

Two of those signals deserve a closer word, because I have watched both be ignored at a cost. A die that breathes — lifts fractionally off the bolster at bottom dead centre — is telling you that something under the lower shoe is not seated: a clamp drawn up short, a shim that has walked, a shut height set a shade low. Left alone, that movement works the fasteners loose; caught early, it is a ten-minute correction. A stroke gone sluggish before any gauge shows it is usually the counterbalance or the clutch asking for attention, not the die at all.

None of this replaces the checklist. It is what gives the checklist meaning — a record with a person behind it who already knew something was wrong before the form asked. The Set-Up Sheet earns its place by the same logic. It is not paperwork; it is the die's memory, and the setter who corrects it the moment a value drifts is doing more for the next changeover than any audit will.

When a plant changes owners, the tooling contract doesn't survive on sentiment — every die, every supplier relationship, and every qualification gets put back on the table. That's not theoretical this year: at least one SA stamping facility has already changed hands under a new owner, while a separate plant elsewhere in the same industry posted its best production month on record in the same stretch. Both are normal. An industry in transition runs at more than one speed at once, and a tooling shop plans for the range, not the headline.

  • Die ownership — whose asset register carries each tool, and who may move it
  • Maintenance responsibility and the spares held against each die

07INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
Ask TheExpert

How do I stop slug pulls from wrecking a good die?

A reader question, answered by the Editor

Slug pulling has a single root cause beneath all of its symptoms: something is giving the slug a reason to cling to the punch face rather than fall clean. I have chased this fault on more dies than I care to count, and the shops that cured it for good were the ones that pursued that reason rather than the symptom.

Begin with lubricant discipline before anything else. A heavy, puddled film acts as a magnet for the slug on punch retraction; a thin, consistent film across the strip resolves more slug-pull problems than any add-on ever will, and it costs nothing. I have seen a week of vacuum experiments undone by the discovery that the roller coater was flooding one edge of the coil.

Correct the lubricant film first. Everything else is a workaround for not having one.

Beyond that, the toolmaker's customary order of attack: angled relief grooves cut into the die wall, creating a retention step as the slug is driven down; a spring-loaded ejector pin placed on the slug's actual centre of gravity rather than wherever there happens to be room; and, on thin stock especially, a clear air path drilled through the punch so that trapped air has somewhere to go on the down-stroke — the same path that later admits vacuum assist should the mechanical remedies prove insufficient on their own.

Two further variables sit beneath all four remedies. The first is cutting clearance: run it tight and the slug is burnished hard against the punch flank over a taller land, so it grips the punch on the way up; open it toward the upper end of the recommended band for the material and the slug is sheared cleaner and released sooner, at the cost of a slightly larger fracture zone. The second is punch-face geometry. A flat face makes full contact with the slug and lets a vacuum form between them; a modest shear or rooftop grind breaks that contact progressively, so there is never a sealed face for the slug to cling to.

The error I encounter most often is not choosing the wrong technique but choosing one and stopping there. A slug that is marginal on lubricant alone frequently ceases to be a problem the moment the ejector is also balanced on the correct point. Layer the remedies; do not audition them one at a time in production — and write down which layer finally held, because the next die of the same family will want the same answer.

08INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
DieScience

Why a deep draw is really just accounting

First in an occasional series on the fundamentals

Every drawn part — a cup, a can, a housing — is the same piece of metal, displaced, not stretched into existence from nothing. The surface area you start with in the blank is the surface area you have to work with at every station after it. Nothing gets added; it only moves. I learned that sentence at a bench before I understood it at a desk, and it remains the most useful thing I know about drawing.

That is the whole discipline: hold the surface area constant, station to station, and calculate backward from the finished height to the blank you need. Skip that accounting and you are guessing at punch diameters instead of deriving them — and a die built on a guess needs rework that a real one would not.

Nothing gets added in a draw. It only moves. Design like you believe that.

Worked Example — One Cup, Three Draws

Target: Ø50mm × 80mm tall, 1.0mm steel — 82mm draw height after a 2t trim allowance. Blank diameter from surface-area conservation: √(d² + 4dh) = √(50² + 4×50×82) ≈ 137.5mm. First draw capped near 55% of blank (Ø76mm); each station after allows a shallower ~78–85% reduction until the target is reached directly at station 3 — no need to overshoot past it. The figure below draws all four stages to scale.

Each drawing station has a maximum safe reduction — how much smaller the next punch is allowed to be, expressed as a percentage of the one before it. Push past that ratio in one step and the metal tears instead of flowing. Thinner material and less forgiving alloys mean smaller steps and more stations, not a shortcut around the sequence.

The blank holder is where the accounting meets the metal. Too little holding force and the flange, compressed circumferentially as it is drawn inward, buckles into wrinkles; too much and the wall, which carries the whole drawing load in tension, thins and tears at the punch radius. Between those two failures lies the working window, and it narrows as the reduction increases — which is the practical reason the first draw is allowed the largest bite and every later station a smaller one, once the flange has been worked and the window has closed a little. I have watched a tryout crew chase wrinkles with holder pressure until the wall let go; the arithmetic would have told them that station was already asking too much.

None of this replaces a shop's own reduction tables, built from its own material and its own presses. But the accounting principle beneath them does not change: know your finishing surface area, hold it constant, and let the punch schedule fall out of the arithmetic rather than out of habit.

09INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
DieScience

Why punches chip — and it's usually not the steel

Second in an occasional series on the fundamentals

Materials keep getting stronger. What counted as "high strength" when I started is now the easy job, and cutting sections are absorbing shock loads nobody designed them for. When a punch begins to chip, the instinct on every floor I have visited is the same: blame the steel. I would examine the press first.

A gap-frame or C-frame press deflects under tonnage in a way a straight-side press does not: the throat opens as load climbs, the ram tips out of parallel with the bolster, and that misalignment — not the metal being cut — is what chips a cutting edge. A servo press helps for a different reason: it can slow the ram at the instant of contact, reducing the shock load rather than striking the sheet at full crank speed. Neither fact reveals itself by inspecting the punch. It reveals itself by observing what the press actually does under load, which is a thing I have watched very few people stop to do.

Examine the press before you re-order the steel. The steel is rarely the actual problem.

Two checks belong before any purchase order, and both cost an hour. The first is a parallelism check with the die out: a dial indicator on the ram face, swept against the bolster at the four corners, under no load and then with a lead or shim check at working tonnage, will show whether the frame is tipping and by how much. The second is the guide system of the die itself — pillars and bushings that have taken a side load once will steer the punch a fraction off line every stroke thereafter, and a chipped edge on one side of the punch only is the signature. Clearance closes the list: too tight a cut raises the lateral load on the edge and drives the fracture up the flank; the recommended band for the material is a starting point, not a ceiling.

Beyond the press, the customary order of attack: when chipping is the failure mode, select a tool steel for impact toughness rather than wear resistance alone — the two are distinct properties, and a steel optimised for one frequently surrenders the other. If the punch was wire-EDM'd, stress-relieve it afterwards; the quench inherent in cutting tool steel under water leaves the cut surface brittle, and omitting the temper leaves that brittleness in the very part doing the work. And a small edge radius, honestly stoned in rather than left as a sharp ground corner, does more for chip resistance than most shops budget the time for. I have never regretted the twenty minutes.

None of this is exotic. It is the order in which you examine things that decides whether the remedy holds or the chipping simply returns in six weeks — press, guides, clearance, then steel, then heat treatment, then the edge itself.

10INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
People &Plants

Remote work: what the trials actually found

First of three — the evidence, both sides argued

Remote work is one of the few workplace arguments to have been settled the proper way: by randomised controlled trials, the method used to test medicines. Volunteers were split at random into office and home groups, measured for months, and the results published and peer-reviewed. I went looking for those numbers because I was tired of hearing opinions, including my own. They now exist for both sides of the boardroom table.

For the employer: in the first big trial (call-centre staff, 2015), home workers outperformed the office group by about 13% — more minutes per shift, more calls per minute in a quieter room — and attrition halved. In the 2024 follow-up on 1,612 professionals, published in Nature, hybrid working showed zero effect on productivity or work quality while resignations fell by a third. A benefit that costs nothing in output and cuts quitting by 33% is not a perk. It is a hard number, and I would put it in front of any board.

Managers predicted hybrid would hurt productivity. By the end of the trial, they'd changed their minds.

Against, for the employer: Microsoft's study of 61,182 of its own staff found the quiet cost of going fully remote — cross-group collaboration fell by roughly a quarter. Teams talked more within themselves, less across the business. This week's output held; next year's ideas got thinner. Hybrid and full-remote are not the same animal, and I have watched people argue for one using evidence about the other.

For the employee: higher satisfaction in both trials, the commute returned to the worker's own life — and the people least likely to quit under hybrid were women, non-managers, and long-distance commuters.

Against, for the employee: the oldest trial found home workers' promotion rate fell for the same measured performance. Out of sight carried a career price. Negotiate visibility along with flexibility.

How to read the trials. The design is what gives these numbers their weight. In the 2015 study, volunteers were assigned to home or office by the parity of their birth date — an even day sent you home, an odd day kept you in — so neither the keen nor the reluctant could sort themselves into the group they preferred. The 2024 hybrid trial used the same principle across 1,612 engineers, marketers and finance staff, with performance reviews and promotions tracked for two years afterwards. A survey asks people what they think happened; a randomised trial measures what did. The distinction matters most where the loudest opinions live — and on this subject that is the boardroom.

Sources: Bloom et al., QJE 2015 (nber.org/papers/w18871) · Bloom, Han & Liang, Nature 2024 (Stanford Report) · Yang et al., Nature Human Behaviour 2021

11INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
People &Plants

The shop floor can't Zoom

Second of three — sector by sector, who can and who can't

University of Chicago economists answered the question no HR seminar wanted to ask: how much work can physically be done from home at all? Their occupation-by-occupation answer: about 37% of jobs — skewing toward the better paid, covering roughly 46% of wages. The other 63% touch material, machines, patients or customers. No video call forms a flange, and I have yet to meet the setter who could clear a misfeed by telephone.

Manufacturing sits mostly on the wrong side of that line, and every reader of this magazine knows why. A press line runs where the press is. Die tryout happens at the die. A misfeed is cleared in person; first-off inspection happens at the tool, not on a screen. The production half of a stamping business is, and will remain, a place you go.

The question isn't "are we a remote business?" It's "which seats actually need to be in this building — and on which days?"

But no stamping firm is only a shop floor. Walk the front office of the same business, as I have in more of them than I can name: quoting and estimating, CAD and die design, forming simulation, scheduling, quality documentation, PPAP paperwork, purchasing, accounts. Much of that is screen work — exactly the 37%.

That split creates a fairness problem worth managing deliberately. If the design office is home on Fridays and the press crew cannot be, the floor notices; I have heard it noticed, in language this magazine will not print. The firms that handle it well are explicit: hands-on roles get flexibilities of their own — shift preference, overtime access, training time — and screen roles get hybrid with fixed anchor days, so the toolmaker can still find the designer at the machine when a section binds. The worst outcome is the unspoken two-class system.

Technology moves the line a little, not a lot. Press monitoring now puts tonnage curves, die-protection faults and counterbalance pressures on a phone, and a maintenance engineer can read a press from a kitchen table at six in the morning. What the phone cannot do is change a bushing. Remote monitoring shortens the diagnosis; the repair still happens at the machine, and so does the apprenticeship — a young setter learns by standing beside an old one, and no dashboard reproduces that.

One honesty note: the trials that found "no productivity loss" were run on coders and call agents, not toolrooms. Nothing in the evidence licenses remote die tryout. What it licenses is treating the office side of a manufacturing business as the office it is.

Sources: Dingel & Neiman, "How Many Jobs Can Be Done at Home?" (nber.org/papers/w26948) · CEPR summary, 2020

12INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
People &Plants

The human ledger

Third of three — quality of life vs the office floor

The spreadsheet argument is settled well enough. The human argument is untidier, and the honest version of it carries entries on both sides of the ledger. I have kept both columns open in my own business, and I have not found a way to make either one disappear.

The quality-of-life entries are real: higher satisfaction in both trials, and the commute — for many the worst two unpaid hours of the day — returned to sleep, family and life. The people who clung hardest to hybrid were the ones with the least slack in their days.

So are the office-floor entries. The informal transfer — the question asked across a bench, the thing you overhear and file away, the older hand who shows you a trick because you happened to be standing there — thins out when nobody is standing anywhere. A trade like ours was built on exactly that transfer; most of what I know that is worth knowing arrived that way, unscheduled. A young estimator can send a quote from a spare bedroom. They cannot absorb thirty years of judgment through a screen.

When the trial ended and workers could choose, half of the home workers chose to come back.

And the most underrated finding in the whole literature is about choice. After people re-sorted themselves by preference, the measured gains nearly doubled. Remote work works best as an option chosen — not a policy imposed, in either direction. The half who came back in the 2015 trial gave the researchers a reason no productivity metric had captured: they were lonely. I do not think that entry belongs in either column. It belongs in both.

The Mr Anon column — three seats reserved

A hands-on trade, a front office, a manager: three real people, anonymised, telling us what flexibility they can actually use, what hybrid changed, and what they predicted against what happened. No invented voices, ever. Accounts to the editor, in confidence.

Sources: Bloom et al. QJE 2015 · Bloom, Han & Liang, Nature 2024 · Yang et al., Nature Human Behaviour 2021

Verify Before Print

Everything below is reported but not confirmed. Flagged, not printed as fact.

  • SA producing "its first local EV by 2026" — aggregator coverage only, no primary OEM or dtic announcement.
  • A claimed post-SCOTUS SA tariff-mechanism change — source trail incomplete; re-verify before use.
  • Isuzu's R1.2bn Gqeberha "investment" that surfaces in search results dates to 2019–2021 — don't let it get misdated as recent.
  • Named individual Nelson Mandela Bay tool-and-die shops — no recent coverage found; NAACAM's member directory is the primary source if the real issue wants to name names.
  • "Full-remote is proven safe for output" — not what the evidence says. The strong 2024 result is for hybrid (three days in-office); the full-remote collaboration warning stands unanswered by any trial of equal weight.
  • Remote-work findings applied to trades — the trials measured call agents, coders and professionals. No trial has measured a toolroom, and the physical constraint answers the question first.
  • The promotion penalty — found in the older full-remote trial, absent in the 2024 hybrid one. Possibly hybrid's face time; treat visibility as an open risk, not a solved one.
  • Company-run studies carry company interests — Trip.com's leadership co-authored its own trials; Microsoft studied Microsoft. Peer-reviewed methods, but independent replication still matters.

14INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
CEOFeature

Decentralised Command

Part one — the boss who "does nothing," and why that's the strategy

Watch a certain kind of CEO for a day and you'll see almost nothing. No firefighting, no barking, no queue at his door. The outside verdict comes fast: look, he does nothing all day — excused, if at all, with ah, but he's the boss, that's why. I have been that CEO, and I have heard both readings from the car park. Both are wrong, and the evidence for why fills two pages.

The idea has a 150-year service record. Prussia's army, too big for one commander to steer, rebuilt itself around a rule: the leader states the intent — what must be achieved and why — and the officer on the spot decides how. That doctrine, mission command, survives word-for-word into current military manuals: intent, mutual trust built on real competence, and disciplined initiative — freedom bounded by the goal, not the script. Its business carriers — a submarine captain who replaced permission-seeking with "I intend to," a general who opened his daily briefing to thousands so the edge could decide — all report the same shape: the leader's job moves upstream, out of sight.

The one phase where the boss doing nothing is the proof it worked — is execution.

And the misreading isn't stupidity; it's measured human machinery. Psychology's "romance of leadership" research shows observers over-credit whatever the visible leader does — and its inverse deflates the quiet one. People rate mere presence as dependability, crown the biggest talker regardless of content, and read busyness itself as status. Meanwhile Harvard's diary study of 1,114 real CEOs found the outperforming type spends its days in cross-function coordination — work that leaves no visible trace on the floor — and team research traces most of a team's performance to how it was designed and launched, not to live steering.

What the doctrine demands in exchange is rarely mentioned: competence first. The Prussian officer trusted to decide had been drilled for years before that trust was extended; disciplined initiative is disciplined because the discipline came first. A boss who hands over the how to people he has not first made capable is not decentralising. He is abdicating, and the floor knows the difference within a week.

There is an honest cost: in controlled experiments, humble, hands-off leaders are rated warmer but less competent — right up until results land. The scoreboard, not the schedule, is the quiet boss's defence. The real audit was never his calendar. It's whether his people speak up, decide, and perform while he's not in the room.

Sources: US Army ADP 6-0 (2019); Marquet, Turn the Ship Around! (2013, self-reported outcomes); McChrystal, Team of Teams (2015); Meindl et al., ASQ 1985; Elsbach et al. 2010; Leadership Quarterly 2020 (speaking-time study); Bandiera et al., J. Political Economy 2020; Zapata & Hayes-Jones, OBHDP 2019. Full panel briefs filed with this issue.

15INSIDE MIC · Aug 2026
CEOFeature

The Handover, Measured

Part two — the evidence, the failures, and the South African test

Does handing over power actually pay? In manufacturing, yes — measurably. A 22-year study of 308 UK manufacturers found empowerment one of only two practices that directly raised productivity, worth roughly 9% in value added per employee; meta-analyses find the effect stronger in manufacturing than elsewhere, and strongest where work is variable — a jobbing pressroom, not a commodity line. The proof-cases run through factories: a French brass foundry run as customer-dedicated mini-teams that outlasted every European rival; a jet-engine plant of 170-plus technicians with one manager, where the only order a team gets is the ship date; a steel giant run from a head office of about 22 people — on hard, uniform metrics. Even the andon cord is this doctrine: authority to stop the line, wrapped in immediate support.

The failures teach the same lesson inverted. The famous bossless experiments that collapsed imposed a rigid system by ultimatum, or discovered that no formal bosses meant no accountable ones. Fake empowerment is worst of all: teams that sense consultation-theatre stop speaking up, and conflict rises. The evidence-backed verdict: hybrid — self-management where adaptability matters, hierarchy where reliability matters.

One SA retailer grew revenue ~390× in nine years after handing power to elected worker teams — and still only 38% of its own workers believed the transfer was real.

Now the South African test. Our SME norm is the exact opposite of this doctrine — founder decides everything, which is one reason so few family firms survive their founder. SA's own research supports devolution, with local conditions attached: ubuntu-aligned leadership is participative and present — the handover must be seen, consensus built in the room, or it reads as absence. And you cannot devolve around organised labour: SA legislated worker participation in 1995 and it died largely unused because it bypassed the union channel — the devolutions that stuck were negotiated through the stewards. In most SA plants there's a further truth: pushing decisions to the floor transfers power across the transformation gap. That's not a boss doing nothing. That's strategy.

What the boss keeps: intent, boundaries and risk appetite, competence-building, the flow of information — and total accountability for everything the team decides. What he releases: the how, the permission queue, and the urge to step in when the team is doing it differently but within intent. That last one is the hardest, and I will add one test of my own, because it is the one the critics never apply: ask what happens when the boss is away for a fortnight. If decisions wait, the handover was theatre. If nobody noticed, it was real — and the car park will call it doing nothing.

Sources: Birdi et al., Personnel Psychology 2008; Combs et al. 2006; Wall et al. 2002; Eurofound FAVI case; Fast Company 1999 (GE Durham); Nucor 10-K; Bernstein et al., HBR 2016; de Vries et al. 2012; Wood & Mahabir 2001; Paul & Zimbler 1989 (Cashbuild); Grutter, Field & Faull 2002; Venter et al. 2005. Semco's famous numbers are founder-narrated — flagged, not printed.
